Neonates of the Giant garter snake emerge from their leathery-shelled eggs with a snout-vent length of approximately 36 cm [Lb = approximately 36 cm], a dimension derived from comparisons with the smooth snake Coronella austriaca, whose hatchlings typically measure about 45 cm. This relatively large size at hatching likely confers advantages in prey capture and predator avoidance from the very onset of exogenous feeding. The yolk-sac larva stage is brief, as the substantial endogenous reserves are rapidly absorbed. Once the trophic switch to active feeding is complete, young individuals enter a juvenile phase characterized by accelerated growth. During this period, they must navigate the dense aquatic vegetation of their freshwater marsh habitats, preying primarily on small fish and amphibians. The initial size advantage provided by their 36 cm [Lb = 36 cm] body length may reduce the time spent in the most vulnerable size classes, potentially influencing early survival rates. Field surveys indicate that neonate survival is closely tied to the availability of shallow, well-vegetated refugia where they can hunt effectively while remaining concealed from avian and mammalian predators.

Adult body size in the Giant garter snake exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism, with females attaining a substantially larger ultimate snout-vent length than males. The maximum recorded body length for adult females reaches approximately 132 cm [Li = approximately 132 cm], whereas reproductively active males seldom exceed 104 cm [Li = 104 cm]. This divergence in ultimate size is a common pattern among natricine snakes, often linked to the selective pressures of fecundity: larger females can accommodate more developing offspring within their body cavity. In contrast, male body size may be more constrained by the energetic costs of mate searching and the need for agility during courtship encounters. The observed values were derived from long-term mark-recapture studies in the Sacramento-San Joaquin Delta region, where individuals were measured upon first capture and then tracked across multiple seasons. These measurements reflect the asymptotic size approached after several years of sustained growth, following the plateau phase typical of squamate reptile growth trajectories.

Under controlled thermal conditions maintained at 18 °C [T = 18 °C], the reproductive output of the Giant garter snake has been quantified in captive colonies. Gravid females produce a single clutch of eggs each year [F_R_i = single clutch of eggs each year], with each clutch containing approximately 17 eggs [N_R_i = each clutch containing approximately 17 eggs]. This combination of modest clutch size and annual reproductive frequency reflects a slow life-history strategy consistent with a relatively large-bodied, long-lived aquatic snake. The eggs are deposited in decomposing vegetation mounds or rodent burrows near water, where the stable, warm microclimate supports embryonic development. Following oviposition, females provide no parental care; the hatchlings must emerge and fend for themselves. The reproductive rate, when considered alongside the species' ultimate body mass and lifespan, positions Thamnophis gigas as a K-selected strategist compared to smaller, more fecund congeneric species. These reproductive parameters were recorded in a laboratory colony held at the steady temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C], which approximates the thermal conditions of late-spring nesting sites in the wild.

The ultimate wet weight of an adult Giant garter snake is substantial, with the largest females reaching a maximum recorded body mass of 1678 grams [Wwi = 1678 grams]. This body mass makes Thamnophis gigas one of the heaviest garter snakes, reflecting its semi-aquatic lifestyle and the energetic demands of producing large litters. The sheer mass of gravid females can exceed that of males by a considerable margin, a disparity that influences their locomotion and basking behavior. Heavier individuals are more prone to predation by wading birds and raccoons, yet their size also allows them to subdue larger prey items such as juvenile bullfrogs. Body condition indices derived from mass-length residuals are often used in field studies to assess habitat quality and prey availability across the species' fragmented range. The 1678 gram [Wwi = 1678 gram] ceiling on body mass appears to be a physiological limit set by the structural constraints of the vertebral column and the metabolic costs of maintaining such a large body in a thermoregulating ectotherm. Long-term monitoring in the Great Valley revealed that only a small fraction of females ever attain this maximum weight.

The lifespan of the Giant garter snake is considerable for a colubrid, with the oldest documented individuals living up to 12 years [am = up to 12 years] when maintained under optimal captive conditions at 18 °C [T = 18 °C]. Males may mature slightly earlier, though behavioral observations suggest they seldom secure mating opportunities until they reach a competitive body size. In the wild, senescence and age-related mortality gradually reduce the population of reproductively active adults, with few individuals surviving to the full 12-year mark (12 years) [am = 12 years] at a temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C]. Conservation efforts therefore prioritize protection of the adult age classes, as the loss of these long-lived breeders can have prolonged demographic consequences.
